en.body:
DC Studios has swung for the fences with **Clayface**, an R-rated horror offering that’s proving to be a divisive but undeniably compelling addition to the Gunnverse. Director **James Watkins**, known for the brutal intensity of **Eden Lake**, channels that same frenetic, terrifying energy into a Gotham that feels both familiar and refreshingly gritty. This isn't the Gotham of polished skyscrapers, but a lived-in, working-class landscape where a young actor, **Matt Hagen** (**Tom Rhys Harries**), claws his way from obscurity to the brink of stardom.

The film kicks off with **Hagen** at the precipice of his career, a trajectory violently derailed by a dalliance with a gangster’s moll. A brutal scene, which showcases the film’s willingness to push boundaries, sees **Hagen**’s face gruesomely disfigured. This, coupled with a false assault allegation, shatters his burgeoning career, leaving him embittered and desperate for a way back. It’s this descent into darkness, fueled by a desperate need to reclaim his life and identity, that lays the groundwork for his transformation into the amorphous terror known as Clayface.

## A Visceral Transformation

**Tom Rhys Harries** is being lauded across the board for his performance as **Matt Hagen**. Critics note his ability to embody the character’s tragic downfall and subsequent monstrous rebirth. The film reportedly leans into its horror elements with a satisfyingly "gross" quotient, delivering scares and visceral thrills without requiring extensive prior knowledge of the DC universe. This approach, allowing the film to stand on its own as a horror piece first and a superhero offshoot second, is a significant draw for audiences weary of overly complex franchise lore.

> "Tom Rhys Harries shines in a messy but distinctive DC horror story." — Rotten Tomatoes

**Watkins**’s direction is noted for its mature handling of the material, infusing the nightmare fuel with an empathetic heart. The neon-hued streets of Gotham become a character in themselves, providing a striking backdrop for **Hagen**’s increasingly unstable reality. The film’s 108-minute runtime ensures a tight, focused narrative that, while perhaps not always taking the most conventional shape, is certainly memorable.

## For the Fans and Beyond

**Clayface** represents a bold move for DC Studios, venturing into R-rated territory with a character not typically associated with mainstream horror. For fans, it’s an opportunity to see a lesser-explored corner of the DC mythos brought to life with a unique, genre-bending vision. The lack of required franchise homework is a welcome change, promising a self-contained and impactful cinematic experience. While some reviews suggest the narrative might not always coalesce into a perfectly defined form, the overall consensus points to a film that is, at its core, effective, exciting, and unafraid to get its hands dirty.

## What's Next

**Clayface** officially hits theaters on October 23, 2026, distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures. With early reviews highlighting its distinctive tone and **Tom Rhys Harries**’s standout performance, it’s poised to be a must-watch for horror aficionados and DC fans looking for something truly different.

content_raw: It’s been a wild year for the movie industry and the world, which might explain why so many folks were nervous about whether DC Studios’ highly-anticipated, big swing of an R-Rated Clayface would be able to deliver the goods. Walking out of director James Watkins’ shockingly extreme, and enjoyable, entry in the Gunnverse, it felt silly any of us ever doubted Watkins or the incredible team both behind the camera or in front of it, caked in appropriately muddy, runny clay. Watkins previously burst onto the scene with the hauntingly brutal “Broken Britain” horror entry, Eden Lake , and almost 20 years later brings the same frenetic, terrifying energy to a specifically nightmarish vision to Gotham—albeit with more of an empathetic and mature heart in this superhero offshoot. There’s a sense of fun here that fits the world of DC and the neon-hued streets of Batman ‘s hometown. As our gateway into James Gunn and DC Studios’ Gotham, it works splendidly, establishing a lived-in, working class world that is familiar and yet unlike any version of Batman’s old haunts we previously watched. Beginning at the precipice of his stardom, Clayface follows a young Gotham actor named Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who has crawled his way up from the gutter to the edge of immense fame. Unfortunately, a night out and some bad choices lead him into the bed of a gangster’s moll Mia (Joana Ribeiro). Her beau is less than happy when he finds out and in a scene that will set the stage for just how far Watkins was allowed to go, Matt’s face is gruesomely sliced and diced by some henchies. That along with some false assault allegations from Mia —a plot point that should have stayed in the first draft —destroy his career, leaving him bitter and desperate. It’s here he finds his savior, Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), an experimental scientist whose research was stolen by a cosmetics company which left her in ruins.  Once the exceptional Harries and even better Ackie are on screen together, the film finds its pace and purpose as it explores the lengths we’ll go to “be the best version of ourselves,” and the chemistry crackles as they try to use her nanites to fix his once beautiful face. That would be a nice silver lining, but Caitlyn is married to John Borrelli (Max Minghella in a career best performance), the only likable and not corrupt cop in the GCPD, who is investigating a series of murders that seem to be connected to Matt’s horrific attack. This tragic romance element is played as a delightful Gotham set Phantom of the Opera tragedy, as Matt tries to understand who he is on the other side of disaster, loss, and of course mad science experiments.  To go much deeper into plot would veer into spoilers but as a horror fan who adores comics, it is quite honestly magnificent to see what Watkins has created here.
